intro.title: CREATE TABLE and types
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Until now the tables were already there. This section is about making them. The database belongs to an events venue that has kept its bookings in one spreadsheet-like table, `ticket_sheet`, and wants proper tables instead.

`CREATE TABLE` names the table and lists its columns, each with a type:

```
CREATE TABLE guests (
  name TEXT,
  email TEXT,
  visits INTEGER
);
```

SQLite has five kinds of values: `INTEGER` (whole numbers), `REAL` (numbers with decimals), `TEXT`, `BLOB` (raw bytes) and `NULL`. Use `INTEGER`, `REAL` and `TEXT` as column types. There is no date type: store dates as `TEXT` in the form `YYYY-MM-DD`, and true/false as `INTEGER` 0 or 1.

SQLite is relaxed about types. A column's type is a preference, not a rule, so it will store the text `'ten'` in an `INTEGER` column. Add `STRICT` after the closing bracket to make SQLite refuse values of the wrong type: `CREATE TABLE scores (…) STRICT;`.

To see a table's columns, query `pragma_table_info`:

```
SELECT name, type FROM pragma_table_info('rooms');
```

`CREATE TABLE` gives an error if the table already exists. `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` skips it quietly instead, which is useful in scripts that may run more than once.

intro.title: Primary keys
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Every table needs a way to point at exactly one row: its **primary key**. Most tables use a number for it:

```
CREATE TABLE guests (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT,
  email TEXT
);
```

In SQLite, a column declared exactly `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` is special: if you leave it out of an INSERT, SQLite fills in the next number by itself, and no two rows can share it. The spelling matters: `INT PRIMARY KEY` doesn't get numbered automatically, and inserting without an id leaves it `NULL`.

Sometimes the data already has a natural key, such as a country code. A text primary key works, but SQLite (unlike other databases) lets it be `NULL` unless you add `NOT NULL`:

```
CREATE TABLE countries (
  code TEXT NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT
);
```

A primary key can also be several columns together. A seat is only unique within its room, so the pair is the key:

```
CREATE TABLE seats (
  room_id INTEGER,
  seat TEXT,
  PRIMARY KEY (room_id, seat)
);
```

`INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT` also promises that ids of deleted rows are never used again. Without it, deleting the row with the largest id lets the next insert take that id. You rarely need `AUTOINCREMENT`, but it matters when an old id must never come back.

intro.title: NOT NULL and DEFAULT
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A table can protect itself from bad data with **constraints**: rules written into the table that SQLite checks on every INSERT and UPDATE. The first two are about missing values.

`NOT NULL` means the column must always have a value. An insert without one gives **NOT NULL constraint failed: guests.name**:

```
CREATE TABLE guests (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  email TEXT
);
```

`DEFAULT` gives a value to use when the INSERT leaves the column out. Defaults are written like values: numbers as they are, text in single quotes.

```
CREATE TABLE tickets (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  seat TEXT NOT NULL,
  status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'booked',
  price REAL NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);
```

The two go well together: the column always has a value, and the usual one is filled in for you. But a default is only used when the column is left out. Writing `NULL` on purpose still stores `NULL`, which `NOT NULL` then refuses.

`NOT NULL` doesn't stop empty text: `''` is a value, not a missing one. To refuse that too you need a `CHECK`, in the next lesson. Defaults can also be `CURRENT_DATE` or `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`, which fill in today's date or time.

intro.title: UNIQUE and CHECK
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`UNIQUE` means no two rows may have the same value in that column. Unlike the primary key, a table can have several unique columns, and `NULL` is allowed (even many times, because missing values are never equal):

```
CREATE TABLE guests (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  email TEXT UNIQUE
);
```

Written after the columns, `UNIQUE (event_id, seat)` makes the **pair** unique: the same seat can be sold for different events, but only once per event.

`CHECK (condition)` refuses any row for which the condition is false. Any condition that works in `WHERE` on that row works here:

```
CREATE TABLE tickets (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  event_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
  seat TEXT,
  price REAL NOT NULL CHECK (price >= 0),
  status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'booked'
    CHECK (status IN ('booked', 'cancelled', 'used')),
  UNIQUE (event_id, seat)
);
```

Breaking a rule gives **UNIQUE constraint failed: …** or **CHECK constraint failed: …**, and the whole statement is refused. One thing to know: a `CHECK` passes when its condition is `NULL`, so `CHECK (price >= 0)` lets a missing price through. Add `NOT NULL` when the value is required.

Text comparisons are case-sensitive, so `UNIQUE` lets both `ana@example.com` and `Ana@Example.com` in. Adding `COLLATE NOCASE` to the column makes comparisons ignore case: `email TEXT UNIQUE COLLATE NOCASE`.

intro.title: Foreign keys
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A **foreign key** column holds the primary key of a row in another table, as `loans.member_id` did in the last section. `REFERENCES` turns that into a rule: the value must exist in the other table.

```
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;
CREATE TABLE events (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  title TEXT NOT NULL,
  room_id INTEGER REFERENCES rooms (id)
);
```

**SQLite only checks foreign keys after `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;`**, and the setting lasts for one connection. Here each Run is a new connection, so start your SQL with it. Without it, `REFERENCES` is written down but never checked.

With the check on, an event in room 9 (which doesn't exist) gives **FOREIGN KEY constraint failed**. So does deleting a room that events still use. Add the parent rows first, and delete the children first.

`ON DELETE` changes what happens when the parent row is deleted:

`ON DELETE CASCADE`, as in `room_id INTEGER REFERENCES rooms (id) ON DELETE CASCADE`, deletes the child rows too. `ON DELETE SET NULL` keeps them but empties the foreign key. Without either, deleting a parent that still has children is refused. Pick what makes sense for the data: a ticket means nothing without its event (cascade), but an event can wait for a new room (set null).

A foreign key can point at its own table: `manager_id INTEGER REFERENCES staff (id)`.

intro.title: Tables from queries
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`CREATE TABLE … AS SELECT` makes a new table from a query's result, columns and rows together. It is the quickest way to take a backup or keep a summary:

```
CREATE TABLE contacts_backup AS
SELECT * FROM contacts;
```

The new table gets the query's column names, so name calculated columns with `AS`. It gets rough types, but **no constraints**: no primary key, no `NOT NULL`, no `UNIQUE`, no defaults. That is fine for a backup or a report, but not for a table you'll keep adding to.

For a proper table, write `CREATE TABLE` with the constraints yourself, then fill it with `INSERT … SELECT`:

```
CREATE TABLE guests (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  email TEXT UNIQUE
);
INSERT INTO guests (name, email)
SELECT DISTINCT guest_name, guest_email FROM ticket_sheet;
```

`WHERE 0` (never true) copies just the columns, with no rows. And `CREATE TEMP TABLE` makes a table that disappears when the connection closes: handy for in-between steps.

intro.title: Splitting data into tables
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`ticket_sheet` is one big table, like a spreadsheet: one row per ticket, with the guest's name and email and the event's title, date, room and price copied onto every row. That causes three kinds of trouble:

**Repetition.** Jazz Night's date and price are stored once per ticket. **Changes in many places.** If Jazz Night moves, every one of its rows must be updated, and missing one leaves the data contradicting itself. **Facts tied to other facts.** An event with no tickets yet can't be stored at all, and deleting a guest's last ticket loses their email.

The cure is to give each kind of thing its own table and store each fact **once**: guests in `guests`, events in `events`, and a ticket as a small row that points at both. This is called **normalisation**.

```
CREATE TABLE guests (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  email TEXT UNIQUE
);
INSERT INTO guests (name, email)
SELECT DISTINCT guest_name, guest_email FROM ticket_sheet ORDER BY guest_name;
```

Fill `guests` and `events` first with `SELECT DISTINCT`. Then build each ticket by looking up the new ids with joins on values that identify a guest and an event (the email and the title):

```
-- This gives an error on its own: it needs the guests, events and tickets tables first.
-- The "All three" example in the sandbox runs the whole build.
INSERT INTO tickets (guest_id, event_id, seat)
SELECT g.id, e.id, s.seat
FROM ticket_sheet s
JOIN guests g ON g.email = s.guest_email
JOIN events e ON e.title = s.event_title;
```

Nothing is lost: joining the three tables gives the sheet back whenever you need it. But a change, such as a new date, is now one UPDATE in one place.

intro.title: Indexes
intro.bodyMarkdown:
To find the rows `WHERE guest_email = 'ben.fox@example.com'`, SQLite normally reads the whole table, row by row. That is instant for ten rows and slow for ten million. An **index** is a sorted copy of one or more columns, with a pointer back to each row, so SQLite can jump straight to the matching ones, like the index at the back of a book.

```
CREATE INDEX sheet_email ON ticket_sheet (guest_email);
```

An index needs a name, then the table and the columns. It changes no results, only how fast they are found, and SQLite decides by itself when to use one. To see its choice, put `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` before a query: **SCAN** means reading every row, **SEARCH … USING INDEX** means the index helped.

```
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT * FROM ticket_sheet WHERE guest_email = 'ben.fox@example.com';
```

An index on several columns, like `(event_title, seat)`, helps searches on the first column, or on the first and second together, but not on the second alone. `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` also refuses duplicates, like a UNIQUE constraint. A **partial index** covers only some rows: `… WHERE price > 0`.

Indexes aren't free: each one takes space and must be updated on every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE. Index the columns you often search, join or sort on, not every column. Primary keys and UNIQUE columns get an index automatically. `DROP INDEX name` removes one; this database already has `sheet_room`, on `ticket_sheet (room)`.

intro.title: Design choices
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Designing tables is mostly a few questions, asked again for each thing you store.

**What are the things, and how do they relate?** Each kind of thing gets a table. One-to-many (a room has many events) is a foreign key in the "many" table. Many-to-many (events and performers) is a junction table with a key for each side. One-to-one, such as an optional profile for a guest, is a table whose primary key is also the foreign key.

**What does each column hold, exactly?** One value per column: never a comma-separated list like `'jazz,live'`, which can't be searched, joined or checked properly. Money is safest as a whole number of cents (`1250` for 12.50), because decimal numbers like 0.1 can't be stored exactly. Dates are `YYYY-MM-DD` text, and true/false is 0 or 1.

**What must always be true?** Write it into the table: `NOT NULL` for required values, `UNIQUE` for things that can't repeat, `CHECK` for allowed values, and foreign keys for links. A rule in the table is checked on every change, by every program, forever.

```
CREATE TABLE prices (
  item TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  cents INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (cents >= 0)
);
```

A short list of allowed values can be a `CHECK (status IN (…))`. If the list changes often or has details of its own, make it a small lookup table and point to it with a foreign key.

  event_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES events (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  seat TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'standing',
  UNIQUE (event_id, seat)
);

SELECT g.id, e.id, COALESCE(s.seat, 'standing')
FROM ticket_sheet s
JOIN guests g ON g.email = s.guest_email
JOIN events e ON e.title = s.event_title
ORDER BY g.id, e.id;
SELECT e.title, COUNT(*) AS tickets, SUM(e.price) AS takings
FROM tickets t
JOIN events e ON e.id = t.event_id
GROUP BY e.id, e.title
ORDER BY e.title;

intro.title: Hard project: Venue booking system
intro.bodyMarkdown:
The venue wants a booking system it can trust. Design it so bad data can't get in: rooms with real seat counts, events on real dates in existing rooms, prices in cents, and tickets with known statuses.

Each challenge starts fresh. Copy your earlier answers forward as the design grows.

challenges.hint: The rebuild pattern from "Changing and removing tables".
